messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Ravi, a forty-nine-year-old military medic, had spent two decades tending to soldiers in field hospitals and clinic wards, but the damage he carried was not from any war zone. It came from the woman he had loved in his thirties, a relationship that ended one night when she turned on him with a fury he still could not explain. She had been drinking; he remembered the sour smell of sweat and alcohol as she pinned him to the floor, her knee in his ribs, her fists coming down on his chest and arms. He was trained to immobilise a combatant, but he did not fight back. He could not. He was certain that if he hurt her, he would be the one blamed. When he finally called the police, they arrived quickly—two officers in crisp uniforms—but after taking statements, they told him it was a “domestic dispute” and left without pressing charges. She faced no consequences. Ravi was left with the memory, and with a quiet, corrosive certainty that something in him must have deserved it.

In the months and years that followed, Ravi’s life narrowed. He stopped wearing the style of shirt he had worn that night—a plain grey crewneck—because the sight of it in his closet brought the scene back as if it were happening now. He could not put the event into words; when his current wife, Anjali, asked what had happened with his ex, he could only shake his head. The sensations were what returned: the sharp pain in his ribs when he remembered, the feeling of being pinned, the smell of sweat. That odour haunted him most. He began avoiding the gym entirely, even though he had always been physically active, because the smell of his own perspiration or another person’s triggered a visceral reliving that left him drenched in cold sweat and shaking. At work, he started to avoid colleagues and patients alike, taking administrative duties that kept him in a back office. He only felt safe in a very limited number of places—his bedroom at home with the door locked, and one supply closet at the hospital where no one ever came. Ordinary sounds, like the click of a door latch or the hum of a fluorescent light, made him jump as if a threat were upon him.

Sleep became a problem because Ravi felt he had to stay alert. He lay awake for hours, scanning for movement, listening for footsteps, his body tense. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was defective, marked by what had happened. Nothing felt meaningful anymore; his work, once a source of pride as he saved lives, seemed hollow. The people who had hurt him—his ex-partner and the system that let her walk free—had faced no accountability, and that injustice gnawed at him more than he admitted.

He only sought help when his avoidance began to fracture his marriage. Anjali had started to cry during an argument, telling him she felt like a stranger. That night, lying in their bed with his back to her, Ravi realised he could not remember the last time he had let himself be fully present. What frightened him most was the thought that he was beyond repair—that the defect he felt was not a wound but a truth about who he was. Still, he made the appointment, and in the therapist’s office, he sat with his hands clenched, hoping that maybe, if he could find a way to speak the unspeakable, something might finally shift.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Authority Presence: Police: The vignette does not describe police presence as a current trigger; police only appear in the past event narrative.
- Known People: Related people: The vignette does not describe any current trigger from related people; only general avoidance of people is mentioned, not specific to known individuals.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

The sensations were what returned: the sharp pain in his ribs when he remembered, the feeling of being pinned, the smell of sweat. That odour haunted him most. He began avoiding the gym entirely, even though he had always been physically active, because the smell of his own perspiration or another person’s triggered a visceral reliving that left him drenched in cold sweat and shaking. At work, he started to avoid colleagues and patients alike, taking administrative duties that kept him in a back office. He only felt safe in a very limited number of places—his bedroom at home with the door locked, and one supply closet at the hospital where no one ever came. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was defective, marked by what had happened. Nothing felt meaningful anymore; his work, once a source of pride as he saved lives, seemed hollow. The people who had hurt him—his ex-partner and the system that let her walk free—had faced no accountability, and that injustice gnawed at him more than he admitted. But the weight of that injustice had also taken on new, more immediate shapes. Now, whenever Ravi saw a police cruiser in his rearview mirror or passed an officer on the street, his heart would slam against his ribs and his palms would go slick with sweat. He was certain they would look at him and see a liar, a man who had deserved what happened, and his mind would replay the moment the officers had shrugged and walked away. He was certain they all knew, that they judged him, that they saw the same defect he felt inside. That night, lying in their bed with his back to her, Ravi realised he could not remember the last time he had let himself be fully present.
